strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: adapting large pretrained video diffusion models into autoregressive, action-conditioned world models.
Vid2World presents a coherent combination of causal temporal attention, causal convolution weight transfer, per-frame diffusion noise levels, and action-specific classifier-free guidance.

Experiments cover two meaningfully different domains—real-world robot manipulation and visually dynamic game simulation—and report substantial gains over the selected baselines, particularly against DIAMOND on CS:GO.

The paper includes useful ablations for mixed weight transfer and action guidance, qualitative failure cases, implementation hyperparameters, and an initial downstream Real2Sim policy-evaluation study.
The manuscript is generally understandable, and its figures effectively illustrate the proposed transformation and qualitative behavior.
weaknesses: The central claim that internet-scale video pretraining improves world modeling or data efficiency is not adequately isolated. There is no training-from-scratch control, no comparison across data budgets, and no analysis of how much the pretrained weights contribute after 100k domain-specific fine-tuning steps.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. The CS:GO comparison pits a 1.1B-parameter pretrained model against DIAMOND without matching model capacity, pretraining, compute, resolution, or inference cost. The RT-1 table imports baseline results from prior work, and its FID comparisons are explicitly acknowledged to have been computed incorrectly rather than being recomputed consistently.

Most quantitative metrics measure similarity to the factual held-out trajectory, not causal action responsiveness. FVD, FID, SSIM, LPIPS, and PSNR cannot establish counterfactual correctness; action shuffling, action-sensitivity curves, state-based transition metrics, or quantitative action-adherence evaluations are missing.

The Real2Sim evidence is preliminary: it covers only one task and three checkpoints with 80 trajectories each, has no competing world-model baseline, confidence intervals, or reported blinded/inter-rater protocol, and exhibits large absolute discrepancies from real-world success rates despite preserving policy ranking.

The claimed generality is demonstrated with only one U-Net video-diffusion backbone. The principal ingredients—causal masking, Diffusion Forcing, frame-aligned conditioning, and classifier-free guidance—are largely established techniques, making the incremental novelty of the combination somewhat limited.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper does not compare against zero/random initialization for newly causalized convolutions, homogeneous versus independent noise training, ordinary action conditioning versus guidance across guidance scales, or variants that separate causalization from pretrained transfer.

The work motivates interactive world models and neural game engines but reports no sampling latency, throughput, or memory measurements; a 1.1B-parameter model using 50 DDIM steps per generated frame may be impractical for real-time interaction.

Reproducibility and statistical reliability are limited by the absence of released-code information, random seeds, repeated runs, error bars, and detailed action encodings. There are also minor specification errors, such as the incorrect conditioning variables in Algorithm 3 line 7.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: converting large pretrained video diffusion models into autoregressive, action-conditioned world models. The decomposition into causalization and action conditioning is intuitive and clearly presented.

Vid2World combines causal temporal attention, causal convolutions, per-frame diffusion noise levels, and frame-aligned action embeddings into a coherent system. The mixed-weight initialization is a reasonable practical idea.

Experiments cover two distinct domains—robot manipulation and game simulation—and report several perceptual metrics, qualitative examples, component ablations, and a downstream policy-evaluation demonstration.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, including training resources, optimizer-related hyperparameters, diffusion settings, preprocessing, conditioning dimensions, and sampling parameters. weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. Causal attention masking, Diffusion Forcing with independent frame noise levels, per-frame action embeddings, action dropout, and classifier-free guidance are largely established ingredients. The main new element appears to be the mixed-weight initialization, but its claimed advantage is supported only by one small ablation and lacks theoretical justification.

The evaluation does not isolate the central claim that internet-scale video pretraining produces a better interactive world model. There is no from-scratch counterpart, pretrained-versus-random initialization study, or comparison against an autoregressive model with the same architecture, parameter count, context, data, and training budget.

The baseline comparisons are substantially confounded. RT-1 baselines primarily generate complete sequences non-autoregressively, while the CS:GO comparison uses DIAMOND with a different architecture, context length, resolution, parameterization, and likely compute budget. Consequently, the large reported improvements cannot be confidently attributed to the proposed transfer procedure.

The RT-1 evidence is less favorable than the presentation suggests. Autoregressive Vid2World is worse than action-conditioned fine-tuning on FID, LPIPS, and PSNR, and only modestly better on FVD. Vid2World-NAR also has much worse FID than several baselines. Moreover, the paper states that baseline FID values were computed incorrectly, making those comparisons unusable rather than evidence of superiority.

The experiments do not rigorously establish action faithfulness or counterfactual reasoning. FVD, FID, SSIM, LPIPS, and PSNR mainly measure visual similarity to one realized future and cannot show that outputs respond correctly to actions. The paper lacks action-shuffling tests, matched counterfactual interventions, action-recovery accuracy, or systematic controllability metrics; Figure 11 is only a selected qualitative example.

The Real2Sim study is too limited to support the downstream claim: it covers one task, three policy checkpoints, and 80 trajectories per policy, with no confidence intervals. Human evaluation lacks the number of annotators, blinding, inter-rater agreement, and handling of ambiguous cases. Merely preserving the ordering of three policies is weak validation, especially when predicted success rates differ substantially from real-world rates.

The ablation study is incomplete and partly contradicts its interpretation. Removing action guidance improves SSIM, yet the text says both components play a dominant role. There are no ablations for pretraining, causal masking, independent noise schedules, action conditioning itself, dropout probability, guidance scale, history noise, or context length, and results are reported only on RT-1 at a shorter training budget.

Claims about interactive or effectively infinite-horizon generation are unsupported. Evaluation rollouts are mostly only 12–15 predicted frames, while the 40-step robot demonstration switches to a fixed sliding window. No long-horizon degradation curves, latency, memory, throughput, or real-time interaction measurements are provided despite discussion of interactive neural game engines.

There are notable specification inconsistencies and errors that undermine reproducibility: the model is described as 1.4B parameters in the introduction but 1.1B elsewhere; the reported latent shape is inconsistent with the stated 320×512 resolution and downsampling factor; Algorithm 2 treats guidance scale 1 inconsistently with its equation; and Algorithm 3 conditions on observations twice, uses inclusive loop bounds, and divides an apparent N+1 trials by N.

Results are presented without repeated seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The selected qualitative figures cannot compensate for this, particularly for stochastic diffusion models and an evaluation involving only 500 CS:GO clips.

The paper makes broad state-of-the-art and generality claims after testing only one pretrained backbone. There is also no stated code release, and the limitations discussion omits important concerns about causal fidelity, evaluation confounds, inference cost, and biases inherited from web-scale pretraining. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

Vid2World combines causal temporal attention, a concrete weight-transfer scheme for temporal convolutions, per-frame noise schedules, and frame-aligned action guidance into a coherent end-to-end method.
The empirical results are promising and cover two meaningfully different domains. In particular, the CS:GO improvements over DIAMOND are very large across FVD, FID, SSIM, LPIPS, and PSNR.
The paper includes useful component ablations: removing mixed weight transfer substantially hurts every reported RT-1 metric, while removing action guidance degrades most metrics.

The Real2Sim experiment goes beyond open-loop video-quality evaluation and provides preliminary evidence that the learned model can preserve relative differences among policies over 40-step closed-loop rollouts.
The exposition, algorithms, hyperparameter table, training budget, dataset splits, and disclosed failure cases make the work relatively understandable and reproducible.
weaknesses: The individual methodological ingredients are fairly incremental: causal attention masking, Diffusion Forcing, action embeddings, action dropout, and classifier-free guidance are established ideas. The main novelty is their integration plus a heuristic temporal-convolution initialization, whose generality is not demonstrated beyond one U-Net backbone.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the claimed advantage of transferring a pretrained video model. RT-1 autoregressive Vid2World is primarily compared with non-autoregressive transfer baselines, while CS:GO uses only DIAMOND, which differs substantially in architecture, scale, resolution, context, and inference budget. Stronger causal video-diffusion and parameter-/compute-matched baselines are needed.

Most evaluation metrics measure similarity to a single recorded future and do not directly establish action responsiveness or counterfactual correctness. The paper lacks controlled action-intervention tests, action-classification consistency, trajectory-level physical metrics, and comparisons across guidance scales.

The Real2Sim evidence is narrow: it covers one drawer-closing task, three related policy checkpoints, and 80 rollouts per policy. Human judgments have no reported blinding, number of annotators, inter-rater agreement, or confidence intervals, and the simulated success rates still differ materially from real-world rates.
No uncertainty estimates or repeated-training results are reported. This is especially important for FID/FVD, the small ablation differences, and the downstream success rates.

Interactive deployment claims are incomplete without sampling latency, throughput, memory use, or quality-speed comparisons. Fifty DDIM steps per generated frame for a 1.1B-parameter model may be too slow for an interactive world model.

Some evaluation choices could inflate or obscure performance: RT-1 metrics include the conditioned first frame, validation-set sampling details are underspecified, and the reported main-table and ablation scores are not directly comparable because they use different training durations. Overall, the evidence supports a promising marginal accept, but not an unqualified accept.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: converting large pretrained video diffusion models into autoregressive, action-conditioned world models.

The proposed pipeline is technically coherent, combining causal temporal attention, causalized temporal convolutions, diffusion forcing, frame-aligned action injection, and classifier-free action guidance.

Evaluation spans three meaningfully different domains—robot manipulation, game simulation, and navigation—and reports strong visual-prediction results, including large improvements over DIAMOND on CS:GO.
The extrapolative weight-transfer initialization is intuitive, supported by theoretical analysis, and compared with shift and masked alternatives.
The appendix provides substantial architectural, optimization, dataset, metric, and inference details, along with qualitative results and informative failure cases.
weaknesses: The central claim that internet-scale video pretraining provides valuable transferable priors is not adequately isolated. There is no comparison against random initialization, in-domain pretraining, or an otherwise identical model without video pretraining.

Much of the method combines established components—causal masking, Diffusion Forcing, frame-level conditioning, and classifier-free guidance. The main novel component, extrapolative weight transfer, gives only small and inconsistent gains over masked transfer: it improves some metrics but worsens FID, with no uncertainty estimates or repeated runs.

The evaluation emphasizes perceptual similarity metrics, which do not establish action fidelity or counterfactual correctness. Action responsiveness is supported mainly by selected qualitative examples; controlled action-intervention metrics or state-based evaluations are missing.

Several comparisons are not cleanly controlled. Models differ in architecture, training data, temporal sampling, prediction mode, and resolution, while autoregressive Vid2World is sometimes compared with single-step or non-autoregressive baselines. Thus, the state-of-the-art claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

The Real2Sim study is small, using only 50 trajectories per policy and one task. It lacks confidence intervals, blinded or multiple annotators, inter-rater agreement, and stronger simulator-based baselines.

Despite emphasizing interactive world modeling, the paper reports no sampling latency or throughput. A 1.1B-parameter model using 50 denoising steps per generated frame may be impractical for genuine online interaction.

Reproducibility remains limited by the absence of a code or checkpoint release commitment, seeds and variance for most experiments, and the high training cost. There are also internal inconsistencies, including describing the base model as 1.4B parameters in the introduction but 1.1B elsewhere, and an apparent guidance-condition error in Algorithm 2, which checks whether lambda differs from 1 rather than 0.

The theoretical bound concerns preservation of a pretrained convolution's output at initialization, but the paper does not empirically verify the assumed local temporal linearity or show that this preservation explains downstream performance after extensive full-model fine-tuning.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: adapting pretrained video diffusion models into causal, action-conditioned world models.
The proposed pipeline is coherent, combining causal temporal attention, causalized convolutions, Diffusion Forcing, frame-aligned action injection, and classifier-free action guidance.
Evaluation spans three substantially different domains—robot manipulation, CS:GO simulation, and open-world navigation—and the reported CS:GO improvements over DIAMOND are large.
The appendix provides useful implementation details, hyperparameters, qualitative results, failure cases, and a modest downstream Real2Sim policy-evaluation demonstration.
weaknesses: The central claim that internet-scale video pretraining provides the key benefit is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison to the same causal architecture trained from scratch, controlled pretraining ablation, or alternative pretrained backbone; only one DynamiCrafter checkpoint is studied. Thus, neither the value of pretraining nor the claimed generality is established.

Action controllability is inadequately evaluated. Most quantitative metrics measure similarity to logged videos and can be dominated by appearance and temporal prediction. The counterfactual action evidence is anecdotal, with no action-recognition, shuffled-action, ignored-action, or paired counterfactual evaluation. This is particularly concerning because the paper acknowledges failures in fine-grained robot control.

Several comparisons are not well controlled. Table 1 mixes autoregressive, non-autoregressive, and one-step systems; CS:GO compares a 1.1B internet-pretrained model against DIAMOND without normalizing model size, pretraining, compute, or inference cost; and the navigation comparison uses materially different prediction formulations. These results demonstrate visual quality but do not cleanly establish method-level superiority.

The theoretical justification for extrapolative weight transfer is not rigorous as written. In the error-bound proof, signed extrapolation coefficients are effectively moved outside a norm without summing their absolute contributions, and scalar kernel magnitudes are used where convolutional operator norms would be required. The vector-valued Taylor argument also assumes a common intermediate point that generally need not exist. Consequently, Proposition 1 is not established by the supplied proof.

The ablations are incomplete and lack uncertainty estimates. They do not separately test causal masking, Diffusion Forcing, pretrained initialization, action injection, or a no-action model. The reported weight-transfer differences are sometimes small or metric-dependent, with no repeated-run variance or significance analysis.

The Real2Sim study covers only one RT-1 task with 50 trajectories per policy. It reports no confidence intervals, number of annotators, blinding, inter-rater agreement, or comparison to another simulator/world model, so it is insufficient to support broad downstream decision-making claims.

Novelty is limited: causal attention masking, Diffusion Forcing, per-frame conditioning, and classifier-free guidance are existing ingredients. The principal new element is a specialized initialization for kernel-size-three temporal convolutions, whose empirical and theoretical support is not yet strong enough to carry the broader claims.

Reproducibility remains limited despite detailed hyperparameters: no code or checkpoints are provided, random split seeds are unspecified, and training requires roughly a week on four A100 GPUs per domain. Ethical and societal implications of interactive generative simulators are also not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: repurposing internet-scale video diffusion priors for action-conditioned, autoregressive world modeling. The combination of architectural causalization, diffusion-forcing training, and frame-aligned action conditioning is coherent and practically useful.

The empirical breadth is unusually strong. Experiments cover real-robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, open-world navigation, and closed-loop real-to-sim policy evaluation, with especially large improvements over DIAMOND on CS:GO.

The comparison among shift, masked, and extrapolative convolution-weight transfer is technically motivated, and the ablation results support the proposed design, although modestly. The appendices also provide extensive implementation details, dataset splits, hyperparameters, qualitative examples, and failure cases.

The presentation is clear and well organized. Qualitative results suggest substantially better long-horizon visual stability than DIAMOND, while the explicit discussion of object substitution and fine-grained control failures is valuable.
weaknesses: The central claim of action-faithful world modeling is not evaluated rigorously enough. Most reported metrics measure similarity to logged videos and can reward models that largely ignore actions. The paper lacks quantitative counterfactual tests, action-shuffling or no-action controls, and measurements of whether generated state changes match specified actions; Figure 13 provides only selected qualitative evidence.

The action-guidance ablation is confounded: models trained with action dropout and sampled with classifier-free guidance are compared against models without dropout or guidance. Evaluating several guidance scales, including zero guidance using the same trained checkpoint, is necessary to isolate the benefit of inference-time guidance.

Some comparisons do not cleanly isolate the proposed method. The 1.1B pretrained model is compared with substantially different world-model architectures, resolutions, and likely inference budgets, while no causal model trained from scratch or causalized pretrained model without diffusion forcing is included. Runtime and per-frame sampling cost are also omitted despite the emphasis on interactive use and the use of 50 DDIM steps per frame.

The theoretical result is not sound as stated for general p. In the intercept-error proof, a norm of a weighted sum with varying second derivatives is bounded using the absolute value of the sum of signed coefficients; the triangle inequality instead requires a sum of absolute coefficients. The notation also treats convolution kernels as scalars rather than using suitable operator norms. Although the implemented p=2 special case avoids part of this issue, the general proposition is unsupported.

Statistical reporting is incomplete. Most results appear to come from a single training run without uncertainty estimates. The real-to-sim study uses only 50 trajectories per policy and does not report annotator count, blinding, inter-rater agreement, or confidence intervals. The navigation comparison also mixes autoregressive and single-step prediction protocols.

Reproducibility is promising but not complete: no code or checkpoint release is stated, and there are inconsistencies such as describing the base model as 1.4B parameters in the abstract but 1.1B elsewhere. Several algorithmic pseudocode details also contain apparent errors or ambiguities, including the classifier-free-guidance condition and Algorithm 3's conditioning variables.
